findings.title: Async legacy writes are cancelled when the request ends
findings.body: Create derives the legacy call context with context.WithTimeoutCause on the incoming request context (same pattern in Delete at line 110, Update at line 135, and DeleteCollection at line 163). A child context is cancelled as soon as its parent is. The apiserver cancels the request context when the handler returns, which is immediately after this method returns the unified-storage result, so the 10s timeout never applies and Legacy.Create/Update/Delete fails with context.Canceled. The safety copy mode 3 exists to write never lands. Those failures are not logged, only turned into a duration metric (and some of those metrics hit the wrong histogram), so divergence is silent. Detach with context.WithoutCancel before applying the timeout so org/namespace/user values are kept but request cancellation is not, and log the legacy error.

findings.title: Unordered fire-and-forget legacy writes can drop or resurrect data
findings.body: Every successful unified write starts a goroutine that mutates legacy with no per-name ordering, version check, or cancellation of older in-flight writes. Delete of "foo" can commit to unified storage and start a legacy delete, then a recreate of "foo" can commit and start a legacy create; if the delete goroutine runs last, legacy no longer has the object unified storage is serving. A stale update finishing after a newer update leaves legacy on old contents. After rollback to legacy those races are user-visible data loss. Serialize legacy writes per object (or drop writes older than the latest unified resource version) and track the goroutines so they can be drained.

findings.title: Legacy update replays the request object and its unified resourceVersion
findings.body: After Storage.Update succeeds, the goroutine calls Legacy.Update with the original objInfo. UpdatedObjectInfo.Preconditions() carries the resourceVersion on the object the client submitted, which in mode 3 was read from unified storage, not legacy. A legacy updater that honors the standard contract will reject the write as a conflict, so the safety copy does not move. Re-running UpdatedObject against legacy's current object can also persist different contents than unified storage just stored (merge patch, generation, managed fields). The previous code forced both stores to persist the object Storage.Update returned via updateWrapper; that was removed and nothing logs the legacy failure. Pass a wrapper whose UpdatedObject returns a deep copy of the stored object and whose preconditions are empty or taken from the legacy object.

findings.title: Successful delete metrics are labeled with the object name
findings.body: On the Storage.Delete success path, recordStorageDuration is called with name, the object name, as the resource argument. The error path at line 103 and every other call in this file pass options.Kind. Successful deletes are therefore recorded on a different series than failed deletes and cannot be aggregated with the rest of mode 3. That argument is the resource label used for the other observations; using the object name creates one series per deleted object and the metric cardinality grows without bound.

findings.title: Durations are recorded on the wrong histogram
findings.body: When Storage.Create fails, the code calls recordLegacyDuration (line 45) instead of recordStorageDuration, so unified create errors never show up on the storage histogram and are counted as legacy failures. Storage.Update's error path does the same at line 129. In the DeleteCollection goroutine, the legacy outcome is recorded with recordStorageDuration (line 166) instead of recordLegacyDuration, so legacy delete-collection latency and errors are attributed to unified storage and the legacy series stays empty. Migration dashboards and alerts will be wrong in both directions.

findings.title: NotFound from unified storage skips the legacy delete
findings.body: Any error from Storage.Delete, including NotFound, returns immediately and never starts the legacy delete. In mode 3 an object can still exist only in legacy (written before cutover, or left behind by an earlier failed legacy write). The client then gets NotFound while the legacy row remains, and rolling back to legacy resurrects the deleted object. The implementation this replaces still deleted from legacy when unified storage returned NotFound. Treat NotFound as success for the purpose of the async legacy delete.

findings.title: Expected NotFound results are logged as errors
findings.body: Get logs every storage error, including NotFound, with log.Error. NotFound is a normal result for existence checks and for idempotent deletes. Delete (line 102), Update (line 128), and DeleteCollection (line 155) do the same. The code this replaces skipped apierrors.IsNotFound before logging. Once mode 3 is on, routine 404s will be emitted at error level and trip log-based alerts. Log NotFound at a lower level or not at all.

findings.title: Legacy create shares the live request object with no copy
findings.body: The goroutine passes the same obj pointer just given to Storage.Create into Legacy.Create, and Create returns the storage result to the handler, which encodes it concurrently. Stores commonly set resourceVersion, UID, and timestamps on the input object and return that same pointer. Legacy create then either sees a resourceVersion and fails admission ("resourceVersion may not be set on objects to be created") or mutates the object while the response encoder reads it, which is a data race. Deep-copy the incoming object before the unified write and give legacy the copy with resourceVersion cleared.

findings.title: Destroy closes both stores while legacy goroutines may still run
findings.body: Destroy calls Storage.Destroy and Legacy.Destroy immediately, but Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection never track the goroutines they start. On shutdown an in-flight legacy write can run against a store that has already been closed, failing the safety copy or panicking, and the process can exit before the goroutine is scheduled. Keep a WaitGroup or worker queue and wait for it in Destroy before tearing the stores down.

findings.title: Mode 3 tests never observe the async legacy write
findings.body: Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection return as soon as unified storage returns and write legacy in a background goroutine. These tests only assert the synchronous return value. Legacy and storage share one mock.Mock, so an On("Create") or On("Delete") cannot tell which backend was called, and nothing waits for the goroutine or calls AssertExpectations. The delete and delete-collection success cases do not register a distinct legacy expectation at all. A change that never calls legacy, or that calls it with an already-cancelled context, still passes. The background mock call can also outlive t.Run and panic if it reports a failure after the test returns. Drive the legacy path synchronously in tests and assert it runs only after unified success, on a context that is not already cancelled.
